evidence.title: Muscle-Specific MEV, MAV, and MRV Baseline Landmarks
evidence.summary: Muscle groups exhibit distinct volume thresholds. Chest MEV is 8.0 sets/week and MRV 22.0; back MEV is 10.0 and MRV 25.0; quadriceps MEV is 6.0 and MRV 20.0; side deltoids MEV is 6.0 and MRV 24.0; biceps and triceps have a direct-work MEV of 4.0 with MRV 18.0. Anterior deltoids receive sufficient stimulus from pressing (MEV 0.0). The optimal 10–20 weekly set range provides the MAV window for most muscle groups. Coaches should seed volume targets per muscle group rather than applying a single global target.
evidence.citation: Schoenfeld et al. (2017). Meta-analysis of volume dose-response. Baz-Valle et al. (2022). Systematic review of weekly set thresholds.

evidence.title: Demographic Volume Scalars for Landmark Initialization
evidence.summary: MEV and MRV landmarks are modulated by experience (novice ×0.80, intermediate ×1.00, advanced ×1.10), age (<40 ×1.00, 40–55 ×0.90, >55 ×0.80), and biological sex (male ×1.00, female ×1.05). These scalars compound: MEV_seeded = MEV_base × α_exp × α_age × α_sex. Female athletes show superior fatigue resistance in high-rep ranges and faster intra-set recovery. Masters athletes (≥45) require caps of +1 set/week progression, 0.85× MRV ceilings, and a deload every 4th microcycle.
evidence.citation: Scarpelli et al. (2020). Individual variability in volume tolerance. Hammert et al. (2023). Baseline-adjusted set progression.

evidence.title: Hard-set credit is graded by proximity to failure, not a binary cutoff
evidence.summary: Hypertrophy rises continuously as RIR falls, with no evidence for a hard RIR-4 cliff. Helm grants full stimulus credit through RIR 2, then tapers 0.9 / 0.8 / 0.5, and zeros from RIR 6 (warmup). Work outside the typical 5-30 rep band still counts at 0.5 rather than 0. Load has a floor at 30% 1RM; there is no 85% upper cutoff.
evidence.citation: Robinson et al. (2024). Proximity to Failure Dose-Response. Sports Medicine. Refalo et al. (2023). Influence of Proximity-to-Failure on Hypertrophy. Sports Medicine.

evidence.title: Fractional (0.5) synergist counting best predicts hypertrophy and strength
evidence.summary: Across 67 studies, counting indirect sets as fractional (0.5) predicted both hypertrophy and strength better than total or direct-only counting. Helm credits primary movers at 1.0, major synergists at 0.5, and minor stabilizers at 0.25, with a 50% weekly synergist cap so rows cannot replace curls.
evidence.citation: Pelland et al. (2025). The Resistance Training Dose Response. Sports Medicine.

evidence.title: Per-Exercise Set Caps and Intra-Session Volume Ceilings
evidence.summary: Meta-regressions demonstrate that hypertrophic stimulus per set drops significantly past 3–4 sets per exercise in a single session as acute local fatigue accumulates. Helm enforces a strict cap of 4 sets per exercise (3 for novices). Research also shows diminishing returns beyond 8–10 total effective sets per muscle group within a single session; working sets beyond 10.0 receive only 0.50 stimulus credit. Coaches should split muscle volume across multiple movement pattern slots rather than dumping sets onto one exercise.
evidence.citation: Meta-regressions on per-exercise set efficiency and diminishing returns. Neuromuscular fatigue studies on intra-session set allocation caps.

evidence.title: Rest Interval Prescriptions by Movement Class
evidence.summary: Meta-analyses show that rest periods of 2–3 minutes for compound lifts maintain mechanical tension and force output across subsequent sets compared to short rest. Helm allocates 180 seconds rest for compound movements (squat, press, row) and 90 seconds for isolation exercises. Session time budgets are calculated deterministically: T_session = Σ(S_j × 40s per set + (S_j − 1) × rest_j) + 300s warmup. Shorter rest degrades volume quality on heavy compounds.
evidence.citation: Meta-analyses on rest interval duration and force maintenance across sets. Grade A evidence.

evidence.title: Linear-Step Weekly Volume Ramp and Double Progression
evidence.summary: A mesocycle uses a linear-step progression from MEV to MRV across 4–6 weeks: V_target(W_k) = MEV + ((k−1)/(N−1)) × (MRV − MEV). For a standard 5-week block with MEV=10.0 and MRV=18.0, weekly targets are 10.0, 12.0, 14.0, 16.0, 18.0, followed by a deload at 50% MEV (5.0 sets). Volume aggressiveness controls step size: Conservative +1, Moderate +2, Aggressive +3 sets/week. Load progression uses Standard Double Progression (reach rep ceiling, then add load) for most compounds and Rep-First Step Progression for isolations.
evidence.citation: PlanKit engine specification v2.0. Progression scheme algorithms by lift class.

evidence.title: Volume-Equated Training Frequency and Hypertrophy
evidence.summary: Meta-analyses demonstrate that training frequency (1×, 2×, or 3× per week) yields equivalent hypertrophy when total weekly volume is equated. However, higher frequencies allow higher total volume without exceeding single-session fatigue limits of 8–10 sets per muscle. Helm distributes weekly targets across exposures: V_session = V_target ÷ M (where M is the number of weekly sessions hitting that muscle). Coaches should not add days for the same volume but may add frequency to accommodate higher weekly totals.
evidence.citation: Meta-analyses on training frequency and hypertrophy when volume is equated. Grade A evidence.

evidence.title: Proximity to Failure Thresholds and RIR Policy by Experience
evidence.summary: Working sets require termination within 0–4 RIR to generate sufficient mechanical tension and motor unit recruitment. Sets completed at RIR >4 fail to provide hypertrophic stimulus and receive 0.00 volume ledger credit. Experience-level policies: Novices train at RIR 2–3 to preserve technique; Intermediates progress toward RIR 1–2; Advanced lifters use RIR 0–1 with planned failure on final isolation sets. During autoregulation, increasing RIR is Tier 1 action (least disruptive) before reducing load or trimming volume.
evidence.citation: Mechanical tension and motor unit recruitment studies. Autoregulation precedence hierarchy (Helm PrescriptionEngine v2.0).

evidence.title: Biofeedback-Driven Landmark Refinement
evidence.summary: MEV and MRV landmarks adjust dynamically from three weekly biofeedback inputs per muscle group: Soreness (S, 0–4 scale), RIR Delta (ΔRIR, prescribed vs actual), and Performance Trend (Δe1RM, 2-week rolling). High recovery (S≤1, ΔRIR≤0, e1RM stable or rising) allows MRV+1 and V_target+1. Optimal adaptive state (S=2, ΔRIR within ±0.5, e1RM stable) maintains MRV while adding +1 set/week. Moderate fatigue (S=3 or ΔRIR>1.0) holds volume constant. Safety bounds clamp MEV to [4.0, MEV_base+2.0] and MRV to [MEV+2.0, MRV_base+6.0].
evidence.citation: PlanKit autoregulated landmark refinement engine v2.0. Dual state machine adjusting MEV and MRV from recovery and performance trends.

evidence.title: Overreaching Detection, MRV Enforcement, and Deload Triggers
evidence.summary: PlanKit establishes two MRV boundaries: a soft warning cap at 0.90×MRV (halve progressive additions) and a hard operational cap at 1.00×MRV (reject all set additions). An overreaching alarm triggers when a muscle logs Performance=4 for two consecutive microcycles while at or above MRV_soft, terminating the mesocycle and scheduling a 7-day reactive deload. Reactive deloads also trigger on estimated 1RM drop >5% across two sessions, persistent soreness (4/4 for >72h), or ARC readiness <0.40 for three consecutive days. Scheduled deloads occur every 4–6 microcycles depending on training age.
evidence.citation: PlanKit overreaching detection and MRV threshold enforcement specification. Deload execution trigger criteria.

evidence.title: Drop Sets, Rest-Pause, and Stretch-Mediated Hypertrophy
evidence.summary: Intensity techniques receive fractional set credit in the volume ledger. Drop sets credit 1.00 for the initial set plus 0.50 for the drop portion (primary mover only, synergist credit 0.00 on drops). Rest-pause/Myo-reps aggregate mini-sets into 0.50 fractional credit after the activation set. Maximum credit per exercise slot with intensity techniques is capped at 1.50 effective sets. Lengthened partials at long muscle lengths count identically to full-ROM sets (1.00) when performed within 0–4 RIR. Stretch-mediated loading yields equal or superior regional hypertrophy compared to shortened ranges.
evidence.citation: Wolf et al. (2023), Maeo et al. (2023), Pedrosa et al. (2022). Lengthened-range hypertrophy systematic reviews and emerging RCTs. Intensity technique set-credit accounting (PlanKit v2.0).

evidence.title: Caloric deficit reduces recovery capacity and MRV by 15–25%
evidence.summary: During a caloric deficit, systemic recovery capacity and muscle protein synthesis rates are attenuated. PlanKit lowers default MRV caps by 15–25%, halts progressive volume ramps once MAV is reached, and prioritises absolute intensity of effort (≤2 RIR) over high volume accumulation to preserve lean mass. Sustained energy deficits impair recovery and elevate overuse injury risk.
evidence.citation: Mountjoy et al. (2018, 2023). IOC consensus statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S). British Journal of Sports Medicine.

evidence.title: Caloric surplus enhances recovery and enables aggressive volume progression
evidence.summary: In a caloric surplus, glycogen availability and systemic recovery capacities are optimised. PlanKit enables aggressive volume progression rates of +2 to +3 sets per week up to the full MRV_hard ceiling. The enhanced recovery environment supports higher training volumes and more frequent progressive overload.
evidence.citation: Helm engine evidence derived from Mountjoy et al. (2018) RED-S consensus and phase-adjustment scaling logic in PlanKit volume model (0.txt §9, 2.txt Phase Interaction table).

evidence.title: Low Energy Availability (LEA) and REDs risk detection signals
evidence.summary: If an athlete logs persistent performance declines across more than 2 microcycles alongside low ARC readiness, elevated muscle soreness (4/4), and suppressed resting heart rate metrics, the engine flags potential LEA risk. The system restricts session volume to MV (maintenance volume), locks RIR at ≥3, and prompts the user to evaluate their nutritional intake.
evidence.citation: Mountjoy et al. (2023). 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). British Journal of Sports Medicine.

evidence.title: Caloric state modifies MEV, MRV, progression rate, session caps, and deload frequency
evidence.summary: Nutritional phase systematically alters training parameters: during a cut, MEV scales up (×1.15: more volume needed to retain muscle) while MRV scales down (×0.80: reduced recovery); during a surplus, MEV scales down (×0.85) while MRV scales up (×1.15). Progression rate shifts from maintenance-only in a deficit to aggressive load progression in a surplus. Max intra-session sets per muscle are capped at 6 (cut), 8 (maintain), or 10 (gain). Deload frequency tightens to every 4–5 weeks in a deficit and extends to every 6–8 weeks in a surplus.
evidence.citation: Helm engine PlanKit Phase Interaction Table (2.txt). Derived from RED-S consensus (Mountjoy et al., 2018) and volume recovery modelling.

evidence.title: Protein intake should be 1.6–2.2 g/kg for hypertrophy and lean mass retention
evidence.summary: Daily protein intake of 1.6–2.2 g/kg bodyweight maximises muscle protein synthesis and supports lean mass retention during caloric deficits. Higher intakes (up to 2.2 g/kg) are recommended during cuts to offset the anti-catabolic effect of energy restriction. Protein should be distributed across 3–5 meals with 0.4–0.55 g/kg per feeding to optimise MPS.
evidence.citation: Morton RW, et al. (2018). Br J Sports Med. PMID: 28698222. Helms ER, et al. (2014). J Int Soc Sports Nutr. PMID: 24864135.

evidence.title: Dietary fat minimums are critical for hormonal health
evidence.summary: Fat intake should not fall below 0.5–0.7 g/kg bodyweight to maintain testosterone production, cell membrane integrity, and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Severe fat restriction during cuts compounds the hormonal stress of caloric deficits and impairs recovery.
evidence.citation: Helms ER, et al. (2014). J Int Soc Sports Nutr. PMID: 24864135.

evidence.title: Carbohydrate intake should be periodised around training demand
evidence.summary: Carbohydrate intake is the most flexible macronutrient and should be titrated to training volume. On high-volume training days, higher carbohydrate intake replenishes glycogen and supports performance. On rest or low-volume days, lower carbohydrate intake aids fat oxidation and insulin sensitivity. During cuts, carbohydrate periodisation helps maintain training intensity while sustaining the deficit.
evidence.citation: Impey SG, et al. (2018). Sports Med. PMID: 29453741.

evidence.title: Body composition change should not exceed 0.25–0.5% bodyweight per week
evidence.summary: Rate of weight loss during a cut should be limited to 0.5–1.0% bodyweight per week, with 0.25–0.5% per week recommended for lean individuals to minimise lean mass loss. Rate of weight gain in a surplus should not exceed 0.25–0.5% bodyweight per week to limit excessive fat gain. Faster rates increase the ratio of fat gain to muscle gain in a surplus and muscle loss in a deficit.
evidence.citation: Iraki J, et al. (2019). Sports. PMID: 31247944.

evidence.title: Creatine monohydrate is the most evidence-backed performance supplement
evidence.summary: Creatine monohydrate (3–5 g/day) increases intramuscular phosphocreatine stores, improving repeated high-intensity exercise performance, strength output, and lean mass accrual. It is safe for long-term use, well-tolerated, and effective without a loading phase (though loading accelerates saturation). Benefits extend beyond performance to cognitive function and recovery.
evidence.citation: Helms ER, et al. (2014). J Int Soc Sports Nutr. PMID: 24864135.

evidence.title: Caffeine is an effective ergogenic aid for strength and endurance
evidence.summary: Caffeine (3–6 mg/kg) reduces perceived exertion, improves muscular endurance, and enhances focus during training. Timing 30–60 minutes pre-training is optimal. Habitual users may experience attenuated effects; cycling off caffeine periodically can restore sensitivity. Excessive intake (>6 mg/kg) increases anxiety and may impair fine motor control without additional performance benefit.
evidence.citation: Helms ER, et al. (2014). J Int Soc Sports Nutr. PMID: 24864135.

evidence.title: Refeeds and diet breaks attenuate metabolic adaptation during prolonged deficits
evidence.summary: Scheduled refeeds (1–2 days at maintenance calories with elevated carbohydrate) and diet breaks (1–2 weeks at maintenance) help restore leptin levels, reduce diet fatigue, and preserve training performance during prolonged cuts. Diet breaks every 4–8 weeks of deficit improve long-term adherence and reduce the magnitude of metabolic adaptation. Refeeds are most effective when aligned with high-volume training days.
evidence.citation: Campbell BI, et al. (2020). J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. PMID: 33467301. Peos JJ, et al. (2021). Transl Sports Med. DOI: 10.1002/tsm2.215.

evidence.title: Hydration status directly impacts strength, endurance, and recovery
evidence.summary: Even mild dehydration (2% body mass loss) impairs strength, power output, and cognitive function during training. Athletes should consume 5–10 mL/kg bodyweight 2–4 hours pre-training and replace 150% of fluid lost during exercise within 4–6 hours post-training. Electrolyte replacement (sodium, potassium) is critical for sessions exceeding 60 minutes or in hot environments.
evidence.citation: Content to be authored with specific citations.

evidence.title: Sleep deprivation impairs nutrient partitioning and recovery
evidence.summary: Sleep restriction (<6 hours) reduces insulin sensitivity, increases evening cortisol, and blunts muscle protein synthesis. It also elevates ghrelin and reduces leptin, increasing hunger and undermining dietary adherence. Nutritional strategies that support sleep include avoiding large meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, moderating evening caffeine, and ensuring adequate magnesium and zinc intake.
evidence.citation: Content to be authored with specific citations.

evidence.title: HRV/SDNN as Autonomic Recovery Marker
evidence.summary: Morning Autonomic Recovery Condition (ARC) scores are derived from sleep-window standard deviation of NN intervals (SDNN), a time-domain heart rate variability metric that reflects cardiac parasympathetic modulation. The ARC z-score is calculated against a 30-day rolling individual baseline: z_ARC = (SDNN_today − μ_SDNN,30d) / σ_SDNN,30d. rMSSD serves as an alternative time-domain HRV metric likewise sensitive to parasympathetic tone. ARC is treated as a systemic fatigue prior that gates total daily volume and cardiovascular strain, not as an absolute indicator of localized muscular force capacity.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L8-9, L40-41

evidence.title: Autonomic Marker Limits for Hypertrophy
evidence.summary: HRV measures autonomic nervous system balance and correlates weakly with acute single-joint force production and localized muscle damage. Autonomic markers cannot capture localized muscular microtrauma, excitation-contraction coupling failure, or joint-specific inflammation. An athlete may register suppressed nocturnal SDNN from psychological stress or late-evening thermal strain while retaining baseline force production. Conversely, systemic parasympathetic saturation can co-occur with severe localized eccentric-induced muscle damage. In hypertrophy, the primary driver is local mechanical tension and peripheral fatigue, not central cardiovascular strain: so HRV-guided protocols that directly scale session intensity are inappropriate for resistance training.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L8-32

evidence.title: Sleep Quality and ARC Relationship
evidence.summary: ARC scores are explicitly derived from sleep-window SDNN, making sleep duration and quality direct inputs to the readiness calculation. Sleep disruption suppresses parasympathetic nervous system activity and reduces SDNN, which cascades into lower ARC z-scores and potentially lower readiness band classification. Poor sleep therefore flows through the Readiness Index formula both via the ARC z-score term (60% weight) and indirectly through the subjective sleep quality rating in the S_sub composite (40% weight).
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L8-9, L35-38, L43-44

evidence.title: Cold Exposure Interference and Travel Effects on Recovery
evidence.summary: Post-training cold exposure (cold water immersion, cryotherapy) may blunt hypertrophic signaling by attenuating the inflammatory and satellite cell responses necessary for muscle protein synthesis, creating interference with the mechanotransduction pathways that drive hypertrophy. Travel-induced schedule disruptions are routed through the deterministic drift policy matrix: sessions logged 24h–48h late trigger calendar shifts and accessory volume trimming; 5+ day gaps freeze the microcycle week index and mark missed sets as SKIPPED_EXPIRED. PPL sequence integrity and intra-muscle rest clamps (48h compounds, 24h isolation) are preserved throughout.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L68-113, L307-309

evidence.title: Readiness Band Definitions
evidence.summary: Four operational readiness bands are defined by the composite Readiness Index (RI). High/Peaking (RI > 0.75): volume pinned to mesocycle plan, no RPE cap, permits higher absolute loads within target RPE/RIR windows but hard-set counts remain fixed. Normal/Baseline (0.45 ≤ RI ≤ 0.75): standard baseline volume (M_V = 1.00), RPE clamped ≤ 8.5 as autonomic safeguard. Low (0.30 ≤ RI < 0.45): volume scaled to ~75% (M_V ≈ 0.75), RPE clamped ≤ 8.0. Depleted (RI < 0.30): volume scaled to ~50% (M_V ≈ 0.50), RPE clamped ≤ 7.0. High readiness does not authorize set volume additions beyond planned mesocycle progression.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L39-47, L300-305

evidence.title: Readiness Index Formula
evidence.summary: The composite Readiness Index merges objective autonomic data with subjective athlete input: RI = 0.6 × ((z_ARC + 3) / 6) + 0.4 × S_sub. The ARC term maps z_ARC (typically ranging −3 to +3) into a 0–1 range by adding 3 and dividing by 6, then weights it at 60%. The S_sub term is the normalized (0.0–1.0) subjective recovery composite incorporating perceived soreness, sleep quality, and stress ratings (each 1–5). The 0.6/0.4 weighting gives ARC majority influence while subjective markers prevent purely autonomic signals from dominating when they conflict with athlete experience. Signal conflict example: z_ARC = −1.60 (Depleted) combined with high subjective scores (4.5/5.0 soreness, 4.0/5.0 sleep) yields RI = 0.48, mapping to Normal/Baseline with an RPE cap of 8.5 as safeguard.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L43-44, L305

evidence.title: Multi-Metric Priority Cascade
evidence.summary: Daily gating follows a strictly ordered hierarchical cascade designed to prevent noisy HRV signals from corrupting training prescriptions. Priority 1: Safety Red-Flags: user-reported sharp joint pain (>4/10), illness, or acute injury triggers immediate movement substitution or rest day recommendation. Priority 2: Subjective Recovery Composite: perceived soreness, sleep quality, and stress (rated 1–5), normalized to S_sub (0.0–1.0). Priority 3: ARC Readiness Score: morning SDNN z-score against 30-day rolling baseline. Priority 4: Prior-Day EWMA Acute Load Residual: quantified systemic fatigue residual from exponentially weighted workload tracking.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L33-38

evidence.title: Intra-Session Autoregulation Precedence
evidence.summary: Intra-session modification follows a deterministic precedence order: (1) RIR/RPE correction: if athlete reaches absolute failure (RPE 10) on a set prescribed at RPE 8, the engine recalculates working load at −5% for subsequent sets of that exercise. If a second consecutive set misses target RPE by ≥1.5 units, remaining sets for that exercise slot are dropped. (2) Fatigue drop-off: if RPE rises by >2.0 units across consecutive sets at identical loads OR completed reps drop by >30% between sets at equal load, the engine terminates the current exercise slot and cancels remaining secondary accessory slots for that target muscle.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L63-66

evidence.title: Low-Readiness Day Modification Algorithm
evidence.summary: When RI < 0.45, the engine processes session modifications through a 6-step ordered sequence, halting immediately once the daily target set reduction factor (M_V) is satisfied. Step 1: Apply RPE Ceiling: clamp all prescribed RPE to 7.0 (Depleted) or 8.0 (Low), recalculating absolute working loads. Step 2: Trim Accessory Sets: reduce isolation/secondary machine slots (Priority 3–4) by 1 set/slot. Step 3: Equipment Swap (if RI < 0.35): replace high axial-load compounds (barbell squat, RDL) with low axial-load equivalents (hack squat, lying leg curl), preserving target muscle mapping. Step 4: Trim Compound Sets: reduce primary multi-joint slots (Priority 1–2) by 1 set, provided remaining daily sets stay ≥ MEV_daily_floor. Step 5: Convert to Technique/Pump (if RI < 0.30 and MEV floor would be violated): all working sets become fixed RPE ≤ 6.0 velocity/pump sets, progression tracking disabled. Step 6: Full Rest Day: if z_ARC < −2.0 AND subjective soreness ≤ 1.5/5.0, OR if prior steps fail to mitigate deficits, session transitions to CANCELLED_REST_RECOMMENDED and drift policy advances the calendar.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L54-62

evidence.title: MEV Floor Protection and Volume Deficit Ledger
evidence.summary: Chronic low readiness risks stranding an athlete below Minimum Effective Volume for consecutive weeks. The Volume Deficit Ledger tracks cumulative per-muscle set deficit: VDL_muscle = Σ(Sets_planned,d − Sets_executed,d). If VDL threatens to drop weekly completed volume below MEV by day 5 of the microcycle, the engine suspends set-trimming on compounds and enforces an RPE cap of 7.5 instead of trimming sets. If low readiness persists for >72 consecutive hours despite RPE caps, the engine overrides daily session execution and converts the remaining microcycle into a Reactive Micro-Deload, resetting weekly volume requirements.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L48-53

evidence.title: Deload Types and Trigger Criteria
evidence.summary: Scheduled deloads occur at fixed mesocycle boundaries: every 6th week for novice/intermediate athletes (5:1 overload:deload), every 4th week for advanced athletes (3:1). Three reactive deload triggers are evaluated daily: (1) Autonomic Suppression: 3+ consecutive Depleted sessions (z_ARC < −1.5). (2) Performance Regression: 2+ consecutive microcycles with ≥3.5% e1RM drop on primary compounds at RPE ≥ 9.0, where e1RM = Load × (1 + Reps/30). (3) Joint Discomfort: subjective joint soreness ≥4.0/5.0 for 4+ consecutive days across movement patterns sharing a joint axis. Severity levels: Single Easy Day (50% volume cut, RPE ≤ 6.0, triggered by single Depleted day with low soreness); Full Reactive Deload Week (50% cut across microcycle, RPE ≤ 5.0, triggered by 3+ days Depleted or ≥3.5% e1RM drop); Regional Deload (reduce affected joint patterns only, normal training on unaffected groups).
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L148-169

evidence.title: Deload Parameter Profiles Across States
evidence.summary: Baseline hypertrophy microcycle: 100% MEV→MRV ramp, all slots active, 70–85% 1RM, 3–0 RIR. Scheduled deload week: 50–60% of peak week sets (clamped to MEV floor), primary compounds retained, 50% isolation trimmed, 60–70% 1RM, 5–4 RIR (RPE 5–6), LISS conditioning only. Reactive deload week: 50% of peak week sets, primary compounds retained, all isolation dropped, 55–65% 1RM, 6–5 RIR (RPE 4–5), active recovery/walking only. Single easy day: 50% of daily target, primary compound only, all isolation dropped, 60% 1RM, 5 RIR (RPE 5), active recovery. Deload set floors use the formula: Sets_deload = max(MEV_muscle, Round(0.50 × Sets_peak_week)).
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L153-200, L165-200

evidence.title: ACWR is displayed; skip-gating stays off unless explicitly enabled
evidence.summary: Helm still computes EWMA ACWR (acute 7-day, chronic 28-day) and shows the ratio. Impellizzeri et al. showed ACWR is mathematically coupled, fails to normalise, and does not usefully predict injury. Ability for ACWR to downgrade a session into a skip sits behind a flag, default off. Deleting real training on a spurious spike is a real cost for no proven benefit.
evidence.citation: Impellizzeri et al. (2020, 2021). ACWR critiques. Sports Medicine / JAT.

evidence.title: Deload Modulation by Nutritional Phase and Landmark Resets
evidence.summary: Energy surplus (mass gain phase): deload sets at 50% of peak volume; high energy availability supports rapid systemic recovery enabling full neural supercompensation within 7 days. Energy deficit (fat loss cut phase): deload sets capped at 60% of peak volume (preserving higher volume for muscle retention signaling), but working loads reduced by additional −5% to account for impaired recovery capacity. Post-deload landmark resets: volume targets reset to MEV_baseline and cumulative hard-set accumulator cleared; initial working loads re-anchored at 92.5–95.0% of pre-deload top weights; 30-day ARC rolling baseline (μ_SDNN,30d and σ_SDNN,30d) recalculated excluding deload-week data to prevent skewing future readiness metrics.
evidence.citation: Autoregulation, Drift Management, and Periodization Policies for Helm. L201-208, L153-154

evidence.title: RPE maps to RIR; stimulus credit is graded
evidence.summary: RPE 6 = 4 RIR, RPE 7 = 3 RIR, RPE 8 = 2 RIR, RPE 9 = 1 RIR, RPE 10 = 0 RIR. Helm does not treat RIR 4 as a cliff. Stimulus credit is full through RIR 2, then tapers, and zeros from RIR 6. Calibration improves with training experience; novices tend to underestimate RIR.
evidence.citation: Robinson et al. (2024). Proximity to Failure Dose-Response. Sports Medicine. Docs/Research/RECONCILE.md.

evidence.title: Movement-Class Progression Matrix
evidence.summary: Progression parameters are matched to movement biomechanics. Squat/Hinge uses Load-First Double Progression (load increments prioritized over rep expansion, +2.5 kg, 6-8 reps, RIR 3→1). Horizontal Press uses Standard Double Progression (+2.5 kg, 8-10 reps, RIR 3→0-1). Vertical Press uses Standard Double Progression with smaller steps (+1.25 kg, 8-12 reps, RIR 3→0-1). Pull movements use Dynamic Rep-Range Progression (+2.5 kg, 10-12 reps, RIR 2→0). Isolation movements use Rep-First Step Progression (+1.25 kg, 12-15 reps, RIR 2→0).
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Progression Schemes by Lift Class

evidence.title: Standard Double Progression Algorithm
evidence.summary: Load (W) is held static while repetitions expand across working sets. Reps increase until all prescribed sets hit the upper boundary of the target rep range (R_max) at or below target RIR. Once achieved, load increments by the movement-class step size (ΔW), and reps reset to R_min for the next session. This ensures progressive overload is earned through demonstrated rep-volume expansion before load escalation.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Execution Algorithms

evidence.title: Rep-First Step Progression
evidence.summary: Used for isolation movements. Load is held static while reps are added set-by-set. When Set 1 reaches R_max at target RIR, reps are then added to Set 2 in subsequent sessions. Load increases only when every prescribed set achieves R_max at or below target RIR. This staggered approach protects smaller muscle groups from premature load jumps that degrade form and stimulus quality.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Execution Algorithms

evidence.title: Load-First Progression for Compound Lower Movements
evidence.summary: Applied to Squat and Hinge patterns. Load increments (+2.5 kg) are prioritized before chasing rep-range expansion. This recognizes that heavy compound lower-body movements produce high systemic fatigue per set; inflating rep counts before adding load reduces the risk of form degradation under fatigue. The rep window (6-8) is narrower than other classes, reflecting the CNS demands of maximal-force production.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Progression Schemes by Lift Class

evidence.title: Stall Detection: 2-Exposure Rule and 10% Micro-Reset
evidence.summary: A stall is registered when an exercise fails to progress in rep volume or load across consecutive exposures at or above target RIR. Exposure 1: log a warning flag, maintain current load and rep target. Exposure 2 (consecutive miss): confirm stall, execute a 10% load reduction (W_new = W × 0.90), hold set count static, reset RIR to 3. The 10% reset sheds accumulated fatigue without abandoning the movement, allowing the athlete to re-sensitize and resume progression from the reset load. Volume-based stall solutions (adding sets) are explicitly rejected in favor of load resets to prevent fatigue compounding.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Stall Detection; Open Decisions §Stall Resolution

evidence.title: Experience-Tier Progression Differences
evidence.summary: Novices (<1 yr): fixed weekly load increments (+2.5 kg on compounds), wide rep windows (6-10 reps), stall detection at 3 consecutive missed exposures. Intermediates (1-4 yrs): standard double progression per movement class, stall at 2 consecutive exposures. Advanced (>4 yrs): micro-periodized wave loading alternating high-load/low-rep and low-load/high-rep sessions across the week, micro-scaled increments (+1.0 kg), stall threshold at 2 exposures. These differences reflect the transition from neural adaptation-driven gains (novice) to structural adaptation requiring periodized variation (advanced).
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Experience-Tier Dynamic Adjustments

evidence.title: Epley Formula for 1RM Estimation
evidence.summary: Estimated 1RM is calculated using the Epley formula: e1RM = w × (1 + r/30), where w is weight lifted and r is repetitions completed. This formula provides a submaximal estimation that avoids the injury risk and program disruption of true 1RM testing. It is most accurate for sets within 0-4 RIR and 5-10 reps. The engine uses e1RM to initialize working loads for new exercises and to track longitudinal strength trends on indicator lifts.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Estimated 1RM Initialization

evidence.title: Historical 1RM Time Decay
evidence.summary: Strength data decays over time following exponential decay with λ = 0.005/day. Logs older than 14 days have their e1RM adjusted by: e1RM_adjusted = e1RM_logged × e^(-λ × (t - 14)), where t is days since the lift was logged. This models the neuromuscular and structural detraining that occurs during layoffs, ensuring that stale historical data does not produce inappropriately heavy initial working loads when reinstating an exercise after a training gap.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Historical Time Decay

evidence.title: Initial Working Load Calculation from e1RM
evidence.summary: When initializing working weights for a new exercise, the target working load is derived from the time-decayed e1RM: W_init = e1RM_adjusted / (1 + (R_target + RIR_target) / 30). R_target is the prescribed rep target, RIR_target is the prescribed reps-in-reserve. This formula reverses the Epley equation to solve for the load that produces the desired rep count at the target proximity to failure, ensuring the first session of a new movement starts at an appropriate intensity.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Estimated 1RM Initialization

evidence.title: RIR Ramp Across Mesocycle Weeks
evidence.summary: Proximity to failure follows a structured ramp from week 1 to peak week. Squat/Hinge 3→1 RIR, Horizontal Press 3→0-1 RIR, Vertical Press 3→0-1 RIR, Pull 2→0 RIR, Isolation 2→0 RIR. This progressive RIR compression mirrors the mesocycle volume ramp (MEV→MRV). Early weeks build work capacity and technique at higher RIR buffers; late weeks drive adaptation by approaching failure, culminating in functional overreach at peak week before the deload.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/2.txt §Progression Schemes by Lift Class

evidence.title: Autoregulation: 5-Tier Precedence Order
evidence.summary: When readiness (ARC) drops or acute fatigue manifests, session parameters adjust in strict priority order. Tier 1: Increase target RIR (2→3) at ARC 0.60-0.69: reduces neural strain while preserving movement volume. Tier 2: Reduce load at target rep range: triggered by bar velocity drop or high RPE. Tier 3: Trim secondary isolation sets at ARC 0.45-0.59. Tier 4: Drop final pattern slot exercise at ARC 0.35-0.44. Tier 5: Truncate session to maintenance volume (2 sets/muscle) at ARC < 0.35. This hierarchy protects the highest-value compound work before sacrificing accessory volume.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/0.txt §Autoregulation Precedence Order

evidence.title: Deload Triggers and Execution
evidence.summary: Deloads are governed by two mechanisms. Scheduled deloads occur every 4th-6th microcycle based on training age and recovery capacity. Reactive deloads trigger immediately when: e1RM drops >5% across primary movements over 2 consecutive sessions, soreness 4/4 persists >72h across 2+ muscle groups, or ARC remains <0.40 for 3 consecutive days. During deload, volume drops to ~50% of MEV (maintenance volume), RIR is held at ≥3, and load is maintained or slightly reduced to preserve neuromuscular patterns without accumulating fatigue.
evidence.citation: Docs/Research/0.txt §Deload Execution Triggers

evidence.title: Nociception Is Neither Sufficient Nor Necessary for Pain
evidence.summary: Nociception is the neural encoding of noxious stimuli via A-delta and C-fibers to the dorsal horn. Pain is a conscious, multisensory output generated by the CNS only when the brain concludes body tissues are in danger. The two are distinct physiological processes.
evidence.citation: Moseley GL, Butler DS. Explain Pain Supercharged (2017). NOI Group Publications.

evidence.title: Central Sensitization in Persistent Pain States
evidence.summary: In chronic conditions, CNS neural circuits become hyper-responsive, producing allodynia (pain from normally non-painful stimuli) and hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain from normally painful stimuli). Pain is then centrally maintained, not driven by active peripheral tissue injury.
evidence.citation: Woolf CJ. Central sensitization: implications for the diagnosis and treatment of pain. Pain (2011). PMID: 20961685.

evidence.title: The Fear-Avoidance Model of Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain
evidence.summary: Catastrophic misinterpretation of pain triggers kinesiophobia (fear of movement), leading to protective avoidance behaviors. Avoidance paradoxically maintains and amplifies threat beliefs, producing a vicious cycle of disuse syndrome, deconditioning, reduced tissue capacity, and worsened pain.
evidence.citation: Vlaeyen JWS, Linton SJ. Fear-avoidance model of chronic musculoskeletal pain: 12 years on. Pain (2012). PMID: 22463735.

evidence.title: Explain Pain: Pain Neuroscience Education Reduces Pain Catastrophizing
evidence.summary: Targeted pain neuroscience education (PNE) shifts understanding from a tissue-damage model to a CNS-protective-output model. Evidence shows PNE increases pain biology knowledge, decreases catastrophizing, and imparts short-term reductions in pain intensity and disability.
evidence.citation: Moseley GL, Butler DS. Fifteen years of Explain Pain. J Pain (2015). PMID: 26051220.

evidence.title: Weak Correlation Between Structural Imaging Findings and Pain
evidence.summary: Many asymptomatic individuals display bulging discs, rotator cuff tears, and meniscal degeneration on MRI. Epidemiological context added to imaging reports reduces threat perception and facilitates faster recovery by preventing catastrophic interpretation of normal age-related changes.
evidence.citation: Moseley GL, Karran EL. Contextualizing imaging findings reduces threat. Br J Sports Med (2020).

evidence.title: Catastrophic Coaching Language Induces Nocebo Effects
evidence.summary: Placebo and nocebo effects are mediated by opposite dopamine and endogenous opioid responses in brain reward circuits. Catastrophic language (e.g., 'your spine is crumbling', 'your shoulder is impinging') can biochemically amplify an athlete's pain experience through nocebo mechanisms.
evidence.citation: Colloca L, Barsky AJ. Placebo and nocebo effects. NEJM (2020). PMID: 32023380.

evidence.title: The Biopsychosocial Model in Sports Rehabilitation
evidence.summary: Modern rehab integrates biological tissue healing with psychological factors (pain catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, self-efficacy) and social factors (coaching environment, season timing, financial pressures). The isolated biomedical model is insufficient for complex pain presentations.
evidence.citation: Ardern CL, et al. 2016 Consensus Statement on Return to Sport. Br J Sports Med (2016). PMID: 26931321.

evidence.title: Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and the Training-Injury Paradox
evidence.summary: Athletes with high chronic workloads show lower injury risk than those with low chronic loads. Injury risk spikes when ACWR (acute 7-day load / chronic 28-day average) rises rapidly. Rehab is not cessation of training but controlled manipulation of ACWR to rebuild tissue tolerance.
evidence.citation: Gabbett TJ. The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med (2016). PMID: 26758673.

evidence.title: Progressive Loading Hierarchy for Tendinopathy Rehabilitation
evidence.summary: Tendinopathy rehab follows four phases: Phase 1 (Analgesia) heavy isometric holds for pain relief; Phase 2 (Strength) Heavy Slow Resistance with 3-4s eccentrics/concentrics for collagen synthesis; Phase 3 (Energy Storage) controlled plyometrics to retrain elastic energy; Phase 4 sport-specific return. Complete rest is contraindicated.
evidence.citation: Malliaras P, et al. Achilles and patellar tendinopathy loading programmes. Sports Med (2013). PMID: 23494406.

evidence.title: Isometric Analgesia for Tendon Pain Management
evidence.summary: Heavy isometric holds (e.g., Spanish squats, single-leg isometric leg press) induce immediate analgesia, reduce cortical inhibition, and preserve muscle bulk. Used in-season or during acute flare-ups to manage pain without irritating the tendon through repetitive loading.
evidence.citation: Rio E, et al. Isometric exercise induces analgesia and reduces inhibition in patellar tendinopathy. Br J Sports Med (2015). PMID: 25716183.

evidence.title: Exercise Regression Hierarchy: Load, Speed, ROM, Complexity, Vector
evidence.summary: When an athlete reports pain during an exercise, modify variables in priority order: (1) Load reduce absolute weight or volume; (2) Speed slow tempo (e.g., 3-1-3-0) to reduce peak forces; (3) Range of Motion restrict to pain-free joint angles; (4) Complexity switch bilateral to unilateral or dumbbell for free joint centration; (5) Movement Vector change angle to shift stress to different synergistic muscles.
evidence.citation: Reiman MP, et al. Exercise progression and regression in rehabilitation. Int J Sports Phys Ther (2014).

evidence.title: Graded Exposure and the Return to Sport Continuum
evidence.summary: RTS is a continuous process (not a single decision) spanning three stages: Return to Participation, Return to Sport, Return to Performance. The StARRT framework evaluates tissue health, psychological readiness, and social/contextual factors. Psychological readiness (fear of re-injury, self-efficacy) is often the primary barrier. Closed-skill testing (hop tests, dynamometry) must be supplemented with open-skill reactive agility and decision-making under fatigue before full clearance.
evidence.citation: Ardern CL, et al. 2016 Consensus Statement on Return to Sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy. Br J Sports Med (2016). PMID: 26931321.

evidence.title: Functional Movement Screen Has Limited Injury Prediction Validity
evidence.summary: Systematic reviews show FMS composite scores are poor predictors of future athletic injury. Injuries are complex, non-linear events driven by ACWR spikes, sleep deprivation, psychological stress, and contact dynamics none captured by a low-load movement screen. Use screening to individualize exercise prescription, not to pathologize movement strategies.
evidence.citation: Moran RW, et al. Do Functional Movement Screen composite scores predict injury? A systematic review with meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med (2017). PMID: 28446455.

evidence.title: Scope of Practice: Red Flags, Pain Severity Referral, and Non-Diagnostic Practice
evidence.summary: Coaches must not provide medical diagnoses. Clinical labels (Rotator Cuff Tendinitis, Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome) must be avoided; use functional movement constraints instead. Pain equal to or above 7 out of 10 during training or joint pain persisting more than 3 weeks despite pattern substitutions requires referral to a licensed physical therapist or physician. Serious pathology red flags (cauda equina, malignancy, infection, fracture) demand immediate medical referral.
evidence.citation: Finucane LM, et al. International Framework for Red Flags for Potential Serious Spinal Pathology. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther (2020). PMID: 32476330.

evidence.title: Unilateral Asymmetry Correction: 1.5x Volume for Lagging Limb
evidence.summary: If a user specifies limb strength asymmetry greater than 15 percent, assign 1.5x set volume to the lagging limb using unilateral movement variants, matching working loads to the capacity of the weaker side. Rehab accessory exercises are tracked separately and do not count toward hypertrophic MRV limits.
evidence.citation: Helm Engine Specification: Constraints and Safety Model (Section 6).

evidence.title: All three energy systems operate concurrently from exercise onset
evidence.summary: The ATP-PCr (0–15s), glycolytic (15–75s), and oxidative (>75s) systems are active simultaneously from the start of movement, with relative contributions shifting by intensity and duration: not a sequential handoff. The aerobic crossover point (where oxidative and anaerobic contributions equalize) occurs around 75 seconds into maximal effort, far earlier than historical models claimed. A robust aerobic base is not antagonistic to strength; it is a prerequisite for recovering between intense bouts and sustaining high training volumes.
evidence.citation: Contemporary metabolic tracing and physiological monitoring studies

evidence.title: Hickson 1980: original interference effect study
evidence.summary: Robert Hickson's seminal 1980 study had participants train 11 sessions per week (6 endurance + 5 strength). Concurrent group matched isolated groups for 7 weeks, then strength plateaued and declined in weeks 8–10 while the strength-only group continued progressing. This birthed the interference effect dogma, but the extreme volume (11 fatiguing sessions/week) created a chronic overtraining state that artificially exaggerated the effect.
evidence.citation: Hickson RC (1980). Interference of strength development by simultaneously training for strength and endurance.

evidence.title: Interference effect is specific to explosive power, not hypertrophy or maximal strength
evidence.summary: Modern meta-analyses spanning thousands of participants show that concurrent training does NOT interfere with muscle hypertrophy or maximal strength development when volume is managed and sessions are temporally separated. The interference manifests specifically in explosive strength and power: rate of force development, vertical jump height, and short sprint speed. The attenuation is most pronounced when sessions are within the same session or separated by less than 3 hours, pointing to a CNS/neurological mechanism rather than peripheral muscle loss.
evidence.citation: Comprehensive meta-analytic reviews of concurrent training literature

evidence.title: AMPK directly inhibits mTORC1: temporal separation is the solution
evidence.summary: Endurance training activates AMPK (the cell's energy sensor), which halts anabolic processes and upregulates mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α. Strength training activates mTORC1, the master driver of muscle protein synthesis. Activated AMPK directly phosphorylates and inhibits mTORC1. If strength work follows endurance work too closely, lingering AMPK blunts the hypertrophic signal. Minimum separation: 3 hours. Ideal: 24 hours for high-volume or intense sessions.
evidence.citation: Molecular signaling studies on AMPK-mTORC1 pathway crosstalk

evidence.title: Untrained individuals experience zero interference from concurrent training
evidence.summary: Untrained or moderately trained individuals possess wide 'adaptive bandwidth': their bodies respond universally to novel stimuli, improving VO₂max and strength simultaneously with no blunting. Interference only emerges as athletes approach their genetic ceiling in a specific trait, where adaptations become increasingly specialized and sensitive to competing signals.
evidence.citation: Training status-stratified concurrent training studies

evidence.title: Sex-specific divergences: trained females show no strength interference
evidence.summary: A meta-analysis of 59 studies (1,346+ participants) found that concurrent training blunts lower-body strength in trained males but produces absolutely no blunting in female cohorts. Females have a higher baseline proportion of Type I oxidative fibers, greater intrinsic fatigue resistance, and lower absolute CNS fatigue from resistance training, allowing faster return to homeostasis between sessions. Females can likely tolerate higher concurrent training volumes and frequencies with less need for strict session separation.
evidence.citation: Meta-analysis of 59 concurrent training studies across biological sexes

evidence.title: Running causes interference on lower-body strength/hypertrophy; cycling and rowing do not
evidence.summary: Running involves repetitive high-impact eccentric muscle actions: each foot strike generates significant microscopic muscle damage and localized inflammation that competes for the same recovery resources (protein synthesis, immune activity) as resistance training. Cycling and rowing are predominantly concentric with minimal impact forces; they deliver cardiovascular and mitochondrial adaptations without the mechanical trauma that disrupts muscle repair. For strength athletes prioritizing lower-body hypertrophy, low-impact modalities are unequivocally superior.
evidence.citation: Biomechanical and concurrent training modality-comparison studies

evidence.title: 90 minutes/week of moderate activity = 14% all-cause mortality reduction
evidence.summary: A landmark study of 416,175 individuals found that just 15 minutes/day (90 min/week) of moderate-intensity activity reduced all-cause mortality by 14% and extended life expectancy by 3 years versus inactive individuals. This benefit holds across sex, age, and preexisting cardiovascular risk.
evidence.citation: Wen CP et al. (2011). Minimum amount of physical activity for reduced mortality. The Lancet.

evidence.title: 150 minutes/week = 20%+ cardiovascular mortality reduction
evidence.summary: At 7.5 MET-hours/week (~150 min moderate activity), all-cause mortality risk reduction exceeds 20% and cardiovascular disease-specific mortality drops nearly 30%. For the strength athlete, 2–3 weekly 30-minute LISS cycling or walking sessions easily hit this dose without generating enough CNS fatigue, glycogen depletion, or mechanical damage to trigger interference.
evidence.citation: Prospective cohort studies on physical activity dose-response and mortality

evidence.title: Polarized training (80/20) outperforms threshold models across all metrics
evidence.summary: Elite endurance athletes across sports (rowing, running, cross-country skiing) naturally adopt a polarized intensity distribution: ~80% of sessions at strictly low intensity (Zone 1, <2 mmol/L lactate) and ~15–20% at very high intensity (Zone 3, >4 mmol/L). In controlled longitudinal studies, polarized athletes show significantly greater improvements in peak power output, lactate threshold velocity, and high-intensity exercise capacity compared to threshold-model athletes. Hard days are genuinely hard; easy days are genuinely easy and promote parasympathetic recovery and fat oxidation.
evidence.citation: Observational research on elite endurance athletes and longitudinal TID intervention studies

evidence.title: Zone 2 'grey zone' training: high fatigue, low adaptation
evidence.summary: Zone 2 (between LT1 and LT2, 2–4 mmol/L lactate, 'tempo' or 'sweet spot') is the grey zone: intense enough to heavily deplete glycogen, elevate cortisol, and induce significant central fatigue, but not intense enough to stimulate maximal stroke volume or VO₂max adaptations. The athlete accumulates massive physiological debt without receiving the corresponding adaptive dividend. For concurrent athletes, replacing grey zone work with polarized Zone 1 recovery and Zone 3 intervals preserves adaptive reserve for strength training.
evidence.citation: Training intensity distribution research and autonomic stress monitoring studies

evidence.title: Respiratory muscle metaboreflex: diaphragm fatigue steals blood from your legs
evidence.summary: During heavy sustained exercise, metabolic byproducts accumulate in the fatigued diaphragm, activating Type IV phrenic afferent nerves. This triggers a centrally mediated reflex that increases sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow specifically to the working locomotor muscles, forcibly redistributing cardiac output back to the respiratory muscles. The athlete experiences sudden, severe leg fatigue that feels like muscular failure but originates from respiratory insufficiency.
evidence.citation: Respiratory muscle physiology and metaboreflex studies

evidence.title: Inspiratory Muscle Training delays the metaboreflex and extends work capacity
evidence.summary: Targeted IMT (breathing against resistance, typically 30 reps at 50% maximal inspiratory pressure) strengthens and hypertrophies the diaphragm over several weeks. Trained athletes show reduced cardiovascular responsiveness to heavy breathing, lower perceived dyspnea, better SaO₂ maintenance, sustained limb blood flow, and significantly improved time to exhaustion: without adding mechanical load or eccentric damage to the legs.
evidence.citation: Clinical and athletic IMT/RMT intervention studies

evidence.title: Self-Myofascial Release improves tissue perfusion and metabolic recovery
evidence.summary: Foam rolling and SMR induce thixotropic effects in fascial ground substance, making tissue more fluid under mechanical stress and reducing internal movement resistance. SMR acutely increases arterial tissue perfusion and blood flow velocity, theoretically expanding lactate transport capacity from working muscle into the vascular system. Integrated into recovery windows between disparate sessions, SMR helps clear localized metabolites and normalize muscle temperature faster than passive rest.
evidence.citation: Fascial physiology and SMR intervention studies

evidence.title: Strength before endurance in same-session concurrent training
evidence.summary: Explosive power, speed, and rate of force development are the qualities most sensitive to interference. When strength and endurance must occur in the same session, the neuromuscularly demanding work (strength/power) must precede the metabolically demanding work (conditioning). This preserves CNS freshness for the quality most vulnerable to fatigue-mediated interference.
evidence.citation: Concurrent training session-ordering studies

evidence.title: Internal focus increases target-muscle EMG amplitude up to 22%
evidence.summary: When resistance-trained individuals consciously focus on the pectoralis major during a bench press or push-up, surface EMG activity increases by up to 22% compared to a neutral or external focus, without decreasing triceps brachii activation. The mechanism is selective enhancement of targeted motor-unit excitation.
evidence.citation: EMG studies on bench press and push-up; Schoenfeld et al. (2018) cited in comprehensive review.

evidence.title: Internal focus yields nearly double elbow flexor hypertrophy (12.4% vs 6.9%)
evidence.summary: An eight-week RCT comparing internal and external focus during resistance training found the internal focus group achieved 12.4% elbow flexor thickness increase versus 6.9% in the external focus group. The mind-muscle connection is a quantifiable mechanism for maximizing localized mechanical tension and metabolic stress, not mere gym folklore.
evidence.citation: Eight-week randomized controlled trial on attentional focus and muscle thickness.

evidence.title: Mind-muscle connection vanishes at 80% 1RM
evidence.summary: The ability to selectively activate a target muscle via internal focus is most pronounced at 20-60% 1RM. As load approaches 80% 1RM and beyond, the CNS must obligatorily recruit motor units en masse per Henneman's size principle. At these loads the selective activation effect vanishes entirely, rendering internal cueing redundant and potentially detrimental to lift completion. For hypertrophy work (<75% 1RM), cue internal focus; for max strength (>80% 1RM), switch to external.
evidence.citation: Load-dependency analysis of attentional focus; motor-unit recruitment threshold research.

evidence.title: External focus reduces antagonist co-activation and improves max strength performance
evidence.summary: The constrained action hypothesis shows that internal focus disrupts the motor system's natural self-organization. Conscious monitoring of individual joint angles or contractions increases cortical resource demand, slows neurological processing, and increases antagonist co-activation: reducing net joint torque. An external focus (e.g. 'explode the bar upward' or 'drive the floor away') allows the CNS to self-organize, increasing both task efficiency and muscle activation patterns. External focus consistently yields superior acute performance in max strength, endurance, and explosive movement tests.
evidence.citation: Constrained action hypothesis literature; motor learning and attentional focus research.

evidence.title: Deep squats are biomechanically safe: half squats concentrate peak retropatellar stress
evidence.summary: Peak retropatellar compressive stress occurs at approximately 90° of knee flexion: the turnaround point of a half squat. Descending past 90° triggers the 'wrapping effect': the quadriceps tendon wraps around the femoral condyles, enhancing load distribution. Continued knee flexion causes cranial displacement of facet contact areas, enlarging the retropatellar articulating surface. Since stress = force / area, the expanded contact area lowers compressive stress. Half or quarter squats with supramaximal weight (enabled by the shorter ROM's mechanical advantage) are more dangerous to passive knee and lumbar tissues long-term.
evidence.citation: Cadaveric joint measurements; retropatellar compressive force modeling.

evidence.title: Posterior pelvic rotation ('butt wink') forces lumbar flexion under load
evidence.summary: If an athlete lacks adequate ankle dorsiflexion or hip mobility, the pelvis may undergo posterior rotation at the bottom of the squat: the 'butt wink.' This pelvic deviation forces the lumbar spine out of neutral alignment into flexion under load, significantly increasing anterior shear forces on intervertebral discs. The coach's decision rule: if the spine remains neutral, deeper is better for hypertrophy (stretch-mediated glute and adductor growth) and joint health. If posterior pelvic tilt occurs, restrict ROM to just above the point of deviation while treating the root cause with mobility work.
evidence.citation: Lumbopelvic kinematic analysis; spinal shear modeling under squat loads.

evidence.title: Sumo deadlift reduces lumbar extensor torque by 25-35% and mechanical work by 25-40%
evidence.summary: The sumo deadlift's wide stance (~70 cm vs ~32 cm conventional) and extreme external foot rotation (~42° vs ~14°) produce a 5-10° more vertical trunk and 11-16° more horizontal thigh at liftoff. The shorter horizontal moment arm from the barbell to the L5/S1 joint reduces lumbar extensor torque by an estimated 25-35%. Barbell vertical displacement is 25-40% shorter, requiring 25-40% less mechanical work. Despite these kinematic differences, peak hip extension moments are remarkably similar between styles. Sumo shifts more demand to knee extensors and hip abductors; conventional demands more from erector spinae and ankle plantar flexors.
evidence.citation: 3-D kinematic analysis; quasi-static joint-moment modeling; force-plate studies.

evidence.title: Flat bench is the optimal primary press; 45° incline drops lower pec activation
evidence.summary: Surface EMG analysis across bench angles (-15° decline, 0° flat, 30° incline, 45° incline) shows the flat bench effectively activates both clavicular (upper) and sternocostal (lower) pec heads. At 30-45° incline, upper pec and anterior deltoid activation increases marginally during 26-50% of the concentric phase, but lower pec activation drops significantly at 45°. Flat bench should remain the primary driver for overall chest development. Inclines are accessory movements for anterior deltoid and clavicular fibers only. Cable pulley systems generate larger maximum shoulder joint moments than free-weight bench press, making them superior for pectoral isolation through full-range horizontal adduction without triceps limitation.
evidence.citation: Surface EMG analysis of bench press at -15°, 0°, 30°, 45°; cable vs free-weight biomechanics.

evidence.title: 90° elbow flare mirrors the Hawkins-Kennedy impingement test; optimal tuck is 45-75°
evidence.summary: Benching with elbows flared to 90° (upper arms perpendicular to torso) places the shoulder in the exact biomechanical position of the Hawkins-Kennedy clinical test used to intentionally provoke rotator cuff impingement. The humerus compresses rotator cuff tendons against the AC joint under load. Safe technique requires elbow tuck between 45-75°. This demands a non-linear, diagonal bar path: the barbell descends to the mid-to-lower chest (sternum) and presses upward and backward diagonally to lock out over the shoulder joints. Coach cue: 'drive the elbows up and back diagonally': this fixes the humerus/trunk angle at its source rather than focusing on hand position.
evidence.citation: Shoulder impingement biomechanics; Hawkins-Kennedy test positioning analysis.

evidence.title: 360° intra-abdominal pressure creates a rigid spinal cylinder; loaded carries train the transfer
evidence.summary: Bracing requires a deep diaphragmatic inhale expanding the abdominal wall 360° against a belt or transversus abdominis. This internal fluid pressure turns the abdominal cavity into a rigid cylinder, drastically reducing compressive forces on intervertebral discs and preventing lumbar flexion under load. Loaded carries (farmer's walk, suitcase carry, yoke walk) are unparalleled for training this capacity: they challenge the core to maintain isometric rigidity while the legs are in dynamic motion. Asymmetric carries (e.g. unilateral suitcase carry) demand massive contralateral quadratus lumborum and oblique activation to prevent lateral spinal flexion, directly transferring to the spinal rigidity required for heavy squats and deadlifts.
evidence.citation: Spine biomechanics research; intra-abdominal pressure and core stability studies.

evidence.title: Pause training dissipates elastic energy and forces high-threshold motor-unit recruitment from a dead stop
evidence.summary: Pause reps (e.g. paused bench at chest, paused squat in the hole) serve two purposes: first, they completely dissipate elastic energy stored in the muscle-tendon complex during the eccentric phase, forcing the CNS to recruit higher-threshold motor units from a dead stop without stretch-shortening cycle assistance. Second, they build isometric strength at the exact joint angle of the sticking point. During the pause, absolute IAP and muscular tension must be maintained: the athlete must not relax. Upon initiating the concentric phase, cue Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT): maximally accelerate the barbell through the remainder of the lift. Because F = m × a, maximal acceleration intent ensures maximal motor-unit recruitment even when bar speed appears slow.
evidence.citation: Link-chain biomechanical models; stretch-shortening cycle and motor-unit recruitment research.

evidence.title: Unstable surface training reduces force output by up to 80%
evidence.summary: When the distal segment is not fixed against a stable surface, the CNS defensively down-regulates agonist motor-unit recruitment to protect the joints. Research comparing isometric squat force output in stable vs unstable conditions shows surface-induced instability reduces joint ROM and slashes force output by up to 80%. While unstable surfaces increase ankle joint sway and small-stabilizer demand, they severely compromise the mechanical loading needed for strength and hypertrophy. If the goal is strength, power, or muscle, stable environments are non-negotiable. Unstable surface training should be strictly relegated to specialized proprioceptive rehabilitation protocols, never progressive overload.
evidence.citation: Isometric squat force output studies; CNS stability-perception and motor-unit down-regulation research.

evidence.title: Resistance training injury rate is 1.0-4.4 per 1,000 hours: safer than field sports
evidence.summary: Systematic reviews of elite weightlifting and powerlifting report an injury incidence of 1.0-4.4 injuries per 1,000 hours of training: vastly lower than contact sports (rugby, football) and non-contact field sports (soccer, track). When injuries occur (predominantly lower back, shoulder, knee), they are almost universally the result of chronic load mismanagement, insufficient recovery, and cumulative fatigue: not singular acute technique failure. Tissues adapt to specific stresses over time; injury occurs when applied load outpaces tissue adaptation capacity over a mesocycle, not because a knee caved slightly on a max attempt.
evidence.citation: Systematic reviews of injury epidemiology in elite weightlifting and powerlifting.

evidence.title: Accept ugly-but-safe form degradation on near-failure sets; distinguish from dangerous breakdown
evidence.summary: As prime movers fatigue, the CNS actively explores alternate motor patterns and recruits secondary musculature. This may manifest as minor thoracic rounding during a heavy deadlift, slight valgus knee twitch out of the hole on a squat, or hips rising slightly faster than the chest. If foundational safety constraints are maintained: neutral lumbar bracing, high IAP, and controlled eccentrics: coaches must accept a degree of form degradation on near-failure sets. The pursuit of perfect form at the expense of progressive overload blunts progression; athletes will never experience the mechanical tension required for adaptation if sets are terminated at the first sign of slowed or labored reps. The distinction: an unsafe rep (extreme lumbar flexion, uncontrolled bouncing eccentric) vs an ugly-but-safe rep (slow grinding squat with minor thoracic rounding). Primary injury prevention focus must remain on systemic fatigue management, intelligent volume titration, and appropriate exercise selection: not rigid perfection on every rep.
evidence.citation: Motor-pattern exploration under fatigue; injury epidemiology in strength sports.

topics.title: MEV, MAV, and MRV Volume Landmarks
topics.body:
Muscle groups have distinct volume thresholds, not a single universal target. Minimum Effective Volume (MEV) is the lowest weekly hard-set count that produces measurable hypertrophy: 8.0 sets/week for chest, 10.0 for back, 6.0 for quadriceps and side delts, 4.0 for hamstrings and direct arm work. Maximum Recoverable Volume (MRV) defines the ceiling beyond which recovery is compromised: 22.0 for chest, 25.0 for back, 20.0 for quads and calves, 24.0 for side delts, 18.0 for hamstrings, biceps, and triceps. The Maximum Adaptive Volume (MAV) window sits between MEV and MRV, representing the 10–20 set weekly range where most muscle groups show optimal dose-response.

These baseline landmarks are not fixed. They seed from demographic scalars. A novice (<1 year) multiplies landmarks by 0.80, an intermediate (1–4 years) by 1.00, and an advanced lifter (>4 years) by 1.10. Age modifiers reduce MRV: 0.90 for ages 40–55 and 0.80 for >55. Female athletes multiply by 1.05 due to superior fatigue resistance, especially in high-rep work. All scalars compound multiplicatively: MEV_seeded = MEV_base × α_exp × α_age × α_sex.

Nutritional phase further modulates these landmarks. During a cut, MEV is multiplied by 1.15 (higher volume needed to retain muscle) while MRV drops to 0.80 (reduced recovery capacity). In a surplus, MEV drops to 0.85 (less volume needed to initiate growth) and MRV expands to 1.15 (enhanced recovery). Coaches should never apply a single global volume target - each muscle group and each athlete context requires individualized seeding.

topics.title: What Counts as a Hard Set
topics.body:
Not every set in the gym contributes equally. Helm uses graded stimulus credit, not a binary hard-set cliff. Full credit applies through RIR 2. Credit then tapers (0.9 / 0.8 / 0.5) and hits zero from RIR 6, which is the warmup row. Work outside the typical 5-30 rep band still counts at 0.5 rather than being discarded. Load is graded against a floor of 30% 1RM; there is no 85% upper cutoff.

Fractional set accounting captures synergist stimulus. A bench press credits pectorals at 1.00, anterior deltoids and triceps at 0.50 each. A barbell row credits lats and rhomboids at 1.00 while biceps and rear delts receive 0.50. Stabilizers like the erector spinae on rows get 0.00 hypertrophy credit (logged for systemic fatigue only).

Two guardrails prevent fractional volume from masking gaps. The synergist contribution ceiling limits fractional sets to at most 50% of a muscle's weekly target; the other 50% must come from direct work. When MEV is at least 8.0 sets/week, at least 4.0 of those must be direct. A lifter accumulating 10.0 fractional biceps sets from rows still needs to do curls.

topics.title: Session Design: Exercise Caps, Intra-Session Limits, and Rest
topics.body:
The engine of a good hypertrophy session is movement pattern diversity, not volume dumping. Research demonstrates that hypertrophic stimulus per set decays sharply past 3–4 sets on the same exercise in a single session as localized fatigue impairs excitation-contraction coupling. Helm enforces a hard cap of 4 sets per exercise (3 for novices). If a muscle needs 6 sets in a session, that volume must split across two distinct movement pattern slots - e.g., 3 sets of vertical pull plus 3 sets of horizontal row.

A muscle group also hits diminishing returns within a single session. Total primary set volume per muscle is capped at 8.0–10.0 effective sets per workout. Any working set beyond 10.0 receives only 0.50 stimulus credit in the weekly ledger, reflecting junk volume that elevates fatigue without meaningful additional stimulus. Session time budgets map to total set capacities: a 30-minute session fits 6–8 sets across 2–3 exercises, 45 minutes fits 9–12 sets across 3–4 exercises, 60 minutes fits 13–16 sets across 4–5 exercises, and 75+ minutes fits 17–22 sets across 5–7 exercises.

Rest intervals directly impact set quality. Heavy compound movements (squat, press, row) require 2–3 minutes between sets to maintain force output and mechanical tension. Isolation exercises operate on 90-second rest. These timers are embedded in session duration calculations: T_total = warmup (5 min) + Σ(S_j × 0.75 min exec + (S_j − 1) × rest_j) + transitions (2 min each). Short-changing rest on compounds degrades the very volume you are trying to accumulate, making it counterproductive.

topics.title: Weekly Volume Ramp and Load Progression
topics.body:
A mesocycle runs 4–6 accumulation weeks followed by a 1-week deload. Volume progresses linearly from MEV to MRV: V_target(W_k) = MEV + ((k−1)/(N−1)) × (MRV − MEV). For a standard 5-week block with MEV=10.0 and MRV=18.0, the ramp is 10.0 → 12.0 → 14.0 → 16.0 → 18.0, then deload at 5.0 sets (50% of MEV, also called Maintenance Volume). The step size is dictated by the volume_aggressiveness setting: Conservative (+1 set/week), Moderate (+2 sets/week), Aggressive (+3 sets/week).

Load progression varies by movement class. Squats and hinges use Load-First Double Progression in the 6–8 rep range, adding 2.5 kg when all sets hit the rep ceiling at target RIR. Horizontal and vertical presses use Standard Double Progression at 8–12 reps with 2.5 kg and 1.25 kg increments respectively. Pulling movements use Dynamic Rep-Range Progression at 10–12 reps. Isolation lifts use Rep-First Step Progression in the 12–15 rep range, adding reps set-by-set before increasing load by 1.25 kg.

Stall detection is automated. After two consecutive exposures failing to progress at target RIR, a micro-reset triggers: load drops by 10% (W_new = W_current × 0.90), volume holds static, and RIR target resets to 3. This unwinds accumulated fatigue and re-sensitizes the muscle. Novices get three missed exposures before stalling; advanced lifters get two. Estimated 1RM is calculated via the Epley formula (w × (1 + r/30)) with a time-decay factor of λ=0.005 day⁻¹ applied to logs older than 14 days.

topics.title: Training Frequency: 2× vs 3× per Week
topics.body:
When total weekly volume is equated, training a muscle 1×, 2×, or 3× per week produces equivalent hypertrophy. The advantage of higher frequency is not in the frequency itself - it is that higher frequencies allow higher total volume without violating the single-session ceiling of 8–10 sets per muscle. A lifter targeting 20 weekly sets for back cannot fit that into one session under the intra-session cap. Splitting across two or three exposures makes the target achievable without junk volume.

Helm allocates session volume by dividing the weekly target by remaining exposures: V_session_base = V_target ÷ M. For a PPL split repeated twice weekly (M=2), a quadriceps target of 14.0 sets becomes 7.0 sets per session. Within each session, volume is distributed across primary compound slots (3–4 sets) and secondary isolation slots (2–3 sets). If a session assignment drops below 2.0 sets for any exercise, that slot is removed and its sets reallocated to remaining slots - single-set exercises are mechanically ineffective.

Coaches should not add a training day just to match a frequency number. Add frequency when volume demands exceed what a single session can accommodate. If a muscle's per-session allocation exceeds 10.0 effective sets, spill the excess into an additional weekly exposure or add a secondary session slot. Frequency is a volume distribution tool, not an independent hypertrophy driver.

topics.title: How Close to Failure Should You Train
topics.body:
Proximity to failure is measured in Reps in Reserve (RIR) - how many more repetitions you could have completed. Hypertrophy requires 0–4 RIR. Above 4 RIR, motor unit recruitment and mechanical tension are insufficient to stimulate growth; those sets receive 0.00 volume credit. The optimal RIR target depends on experience: novices train at RIR 2–3 to protect movement mechanics while building work capacity; intermediates progress toward RIR 1–2; advanced lifters use RIR 0–1 with planned failure on final isolation sets only.

Autoregulation adjusts RIR before touching load or volume. The five-tier precedence order is: Tier 1 - increase target RIR (e.g., 2→3 RIR) when ARC readiness is 0.60–0.69. Tier 2 - reduce load at the target rep range if bar velocity drops or RPE spikes. Tier 3 - trim secondary isolation sets when ARC is 0.45–0.59. Tier 4 - drop the final pattern slot exercise at ARC 0.35–0.44. Tier 5 - truncate to Maintenance Volume (2 sets/muscle) at ARC <0.35. Increasing RIR is always the first and least disruptive adjustment, preserving movement execution and volume while reducing neurological strain.

A critical floor protection prevents chronic undertraining. If readiness gating depresses actual volume below MEV for two consecutive microcycles, the engine locks volume at exact MEV targets, forces RIR ≥3, and suspends dynamic readiness reductions. This ensures the athlete continues to receive a growth stimulus even during periods of compromised recovery.

topics.title: Biofeedback Titration and Overreaching Detection
topics.body:
Volume landmarks are not static. Each microcycle, PlanKit processes three biofeedback inputs per muscle group: Soreness (S, 0–4 scale where 0=none, 4=severe and impairing), RIR Delta (ΔRIR, the gap between prescribed and actual RIR), and Performance Trend (Δe1RM over a 2-week rolling window). These feed a state machine with four recovery states. High Recovery (S≤1, ΔRIR≤0, e1RM stable or rising) increases MRV by 1.0 and adds +1 set/week. Optimal Adaptive (S=2, ΔRIR within ±0.5, e1RM stable) maintains MRV while adding +1 set/week. Moderate Fatigue (S=3 or ΔRIR>1.0) holds volume constant. Overreaching (S=4 or Δe1RM <−2.0% across 2 consecutive weeks) drops MRV by 2.0, MEV by 1.0, and V_target by 2.0, triggering an early deload evaluation.

MEV and MRV are safety-bounded: MEV cannot drop below 4.0 or exceed MEV_base + 2.0; MRV cannot drop below MEV + 2.0 or exceed MRV_base + 6.0. These boundaries prevent the engine from ratcheting an athlete into either zero stimulus or unsustainable volume.

Overreaching detection uses two MRV thresholds. The soft warning cap at 0.90×MRV halves progressive volume additions and alerts the athlete that recovery capacity is saturating. The hard operational cap at 1.00×MRV strictly rejects all set additions. If a muscle group logs Performance=4 for two consecutive microcycles while operating at or above the soft cap, the engine terminates the active mesocycle and schedules a 7-day reactive deload. Reactive deloads also fire on estimated 1RM drops >5% across two sessions, persistent soreness (4/4 for >72 hours across ≥2 muscle groups), or ARC readiness <0.40 for three consecutive days.

topics.title: Drop Sets, Rest-Pause, and Stretch-Mediated Hypertrophy
topics.body:
Intensity techniques extend a set's stimulus but do not multiply set credit. Drop sets log 1.00 for the initial set (performed at 0–2 RIR) plus 0.50 for the drop portion - applied to the primary mover only; synergists receive 0.00 on the drop. Rest-pause and Myo-reps log 1.00 for the activation set plus 0.50 aggregated from the 3–4 mini-sets. A single exercise slot using either technique cannot exceed 1.50 total effective sets toward the primary target muscle, preventing arbitrary volume inflation. These techniques increase per-set stimulus density but do not replace additional working sets.

Lengthened partials - sets performed exclusively in the stretched portion of a movement - count identically to full-ROM sets (1.00) when executed within 0–4 RIR at long muscle lengths. Research demonstrates that loading extended muscle lengths yields equal or superior regional hypertrophy compared to shortened ranges. The engine records a length_bias field per exercise (LENGTHENED, SHORTENED, FULL) and applies a lengthened_partial_hypertrophy_modifier of 1.08 in its JSON exercise definitions.

When an athlete selects the Stretch_Focused exercise selection bias, the engine prioritizes exercises with long muscle length resistance profiles (e.g., seated leg curls over lying leg curls for hamstrings, incline curls over preacher curls for biceps). This bias is a ranking weight applied during exercise slot selection, not a volume or load modifier. Coaches should view intensity techniques and stretch-focused exercise selection as tools within a volume framework, not replacements for adequate hard-set totals.

topics.title: Caloric State and Training Parameters
topics.body:
An athlete's nutritional phase: cut (deficit), maintain (eucaloric), or gain (surplus): directly alters recovery capacity and therefore every volume landmark in the training engine. This is not a suggestion layer; it is a mechanical adjustment the engine applies automatically.

During a caloric deficit, systemic recovery is impaired.
