The engine scales MRV down by 15–25%, halts progressive volume ramps at MAV rather than MRV, and prioritises intensity (≤2 RIR) over volume accumulation. This preserves the anabolic signal per set while reducing total fatigue. MEV is raised (×1.15) because more volume is required to retain muscle when energy is restricted. Max sets per muscle per session are capped at 6, and deloads come every 4–5 weeks.

During a caloric surplus, the opposite occurs: recovery capacity is enhanced, MRV scales up (×1.15), MEV falls (×0.85) because less volume is needed to initiate growth, progression rates become aggressive (+2 to +3 sets/week), session caps rise to 10 sets per muscle, and deload frequency extends to every 6–8 weeks. The maintenance phase sits at baseline (×1.00) with standard double progression and 8-set session caps.

These scalars are applied at mesocycle compilation and are not user-facing toggles: they are structural parameters that reflect the biological reality that you cannot train a calorie-restricted body the same way you train a well-fed one.

topics.title: Low Energy Availability and REDs Risk
topics.body:
Low Energy Availability (LEA) occurs when energy intake is insufficient to support both exercise expenditure and basic physiological function. It is the underlying cause of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), a syndrome affecting metabolic rate, bone health, immunity, and reproductive function.

The engine monitors for LEA risk signals automatically. If an athlete logs persistent performance declines across more than 2 consecutive microcycles paired with low ARC readiness scores, elevated muscle soreness (4/4), and suppressed resting heart rate, the system flags potential LEA. When flagged, the engine forcibly restricts session volume to maintenance volume (MV), locks target RIR at ≥3, and prompts the athlete to evaluate their nutritional intake.

LEA is not the same as a planned caloric deficit. A planned deficit is intentional, rate-limited, and monitored. LEA is often unintentional: the athlete is simply not eating enough to fuel their training: and leads to a cascade of negative outcomes that training cannot outrun. The only fix is increased energy intake.

topics.title: Macro Partitioning: Protein, Fat, and Carbohydrate
topics.body:
Protein is the highest-priority macronutrient for athletes. Target 1.6–2.2 g/kg bodyweight daily, distributed across 3–5 meals with roughly 0.4–0.55 g/kg per feeding to repeatedly spike muscle protein synthesis. Higher intakes (upper end of the range) are recommended during caloric deficits to offset the catabolic pressure of energy restriction. Protein quality matters: prioritise complete sources (animal proteins, soy) with high leucine content (≥2.5 g per meal) to maximally stimulate MPS.

Dietary fat must not fall below 0.5–0.7 g/kg bodyweight. Fat is essential for testosterone production, cell membrane integrity, and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Severe fat restriction during a cut compounds the hormonal stress of the deficit and impairs recovery. The remainder of fat intake beyond this floor depends on personal preference and adherence.

Carbohydrate is the most flexible macro and should be periodised around training demand. Higher training days warrant higher carbohydrate intake to replenish glycogen and support performance. Rest days or low-volume days can be lower to improve insulin sensitivity. During a cut, carbohydrate periodisation helps maintain training intensity while sustaining the deficit. Total carb intake fills the remaining calorie budget after protein and fat targets are satisfied.

topics.title: Rate Limits for Cutting and Gaining
topics.body:
The maximum sustainable rate of body composition change is constrained by biology, not willpower. For lean individuals, weight loss during a cut should not exceed 0.5–1.0% of bodyweight per week, with 0.25–0.5% per week recommended. Faster cuts increase the proportion of weight lost from lean mass rather than fat, slow metabolic rate more aggressively, and degrade training performance and recovery.

Weight gain in a surplus should similarly not exceed 0.25–0.5% bodyweight per week. Beyond this rate, the ratio of fat gain to muscle gain deteriorates sharply. Since muscle protein synthesis has a finite ceiling regardless of energy surplus, excess calories beyond what supports MPS are partitioned to adipose tissue. A smaller surplus sustained for longer produces a better muscle-to-fat gain ratio than an aggressive surplus.

The engine phase table (gain ×0.85 MEV, cut ×1.15 MEV) reflects the biological reality that rate-limited changes create the most favourable environment for body recomposition. These are not prescriptive rates enforced by the engine but coaching guidelines the system can surface when an athlete's logged weight trend exceeds them.

topics.title: Peri-Workout Nutrition and Timing
topics.body:
Peri-workout nutrition encompasses the meals consumed before, during, and after training. The primary goal is to fuel performance and initiate recovery without causing gastrointestinal distress during the session.

The pre-training meal (1–3 hours before) should contain moderate protein (20–40 g) and carbohydrate, with fat kept low to speed gastric emptying. A liquid or easily digestible option is preferred closer to training. Intra-workout nutrition is generally unnecessary for sessions under 60 minutes unless training fasted; for longer sessions, 30–60 g carbohydrate per hour can sustain performance.

Post-training, the 'anabolic window' is wider than often claimed. Total daily protein intake and distribution across meals matters more than immediate post-workout timing. However, consuming 20–40 g of protein within 2 hours post-training is a practical habit that ensures MPS stimulation. Adding carbohydrate post-training accelerates glycogen resynthesis, which is most critical when training the same muscle group within 24 hours.

Nutrient timing is a refinement layer, not a replacement for total daily intake. An athlete who hits protein and calorie targets but eats at irregular times will outperform an athlete with perfect timing who undereats.

topics.title: Evidence-Based Supplements
topics.body:
Most supplements marketed to athletes lack robust evidence. Three stand out with strong, replicated support and low risk profiles.

Creatine monohydrate (3–5 g/day) is the most thoroughly researched performance supplement. It increases intramuscular phosphocreatine stores, improving repeated high-intensity effort, strength, and lean mass accrual. It is safe for long-term use. A loading phase (20 g/day for 5–7 days) accelerates saturation but is not required; consistent daily dosing achieves the same result over 3–4 weeks. Benefits extend to cognitive function, making it relevant during periods of sleep restriction or high stress.

Caffeine (3–6 mg/kg, 30–60 minutes pre-training) reduces perceived exertion, improves muscular endurance, and sharpens focus. Effects are more pronounced in non-habitual users; chronic high intake attenuates response. Cycling off caffeine periodically restores sensitivity. Doses exceeding 6 mg/kg increase anxiety and jitter without additional performance benefit.

Beta-alanine (3–6 g/day) elevates intramuscular carnosine, buffering hydrogen ion accumulation during high-intensity efforts lasting 60–240 seconds. It is most relevant for athletes performing repeated sprint or high-rep training. Paraesthesia (tingling) is a benign side effect that can be mitigated with split dosing or sustained-release formulations.

Protein powder (whey or plant-based blends) is not a supplement in the ergogenic sense: it is a convenience food that helps athletes hit daily protein targets. It offers no benefit beyond equivalent protein from whole food, but its practicality for peri-workout use and meal gaps makes it a staple tool.

topics.title: Nutrition-Supported Recovery: Sleep, Hydration, Refeeds, and Diet Breaks
topics.body:
Recovery is a nutritional event as much as a training event. Three domains interact directly with the engine's readiness and progression systems.

Hydration status directly impacts strength, endurance, and cognitive function. Even mild dehydration (2% body mass loss) measurably impairs performance. Athletes should consume 5–10 mL/kg bodyweight 2–4 hours pre-training and replace 150% of fluid lost during exercise within 4–6 hours post-training. Electrolyte replacement (sodium and potassium) is critical for sessions exceeding 60 minutes or training in hot environments.

Sleep-nutrition interaction is bidirectional. Sleep restriction below 6 hours reduces insulin sensitivity, elevates evening cortisol, blunts MPS, and disrupts appetite-regulating hormones (elevated ghrelin, reduced leptin): making dietary adherence harder. Nutritional strategies that support sleep include avoiding large meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, moderating evening caffeine intake, and ensuring adequate magnesium and zinc. The engine already scales volume when ARC readiness is depressed by poor sleep; nutrition amplifies or mitigates the root cause.

Refeeds and diet breaks are tools for prolonged deficits. A refeed (1–2 days at maintenance calories with elevated carbohydrate) restores leptin and glycogen, improving training quality and psychological adherence. A diet break (1–2 weeks at maintenance) every 4–8 weeks of deficit reduces metabolic adaptation and preserves lean mass. These are particularly relevant when the engine is operating in cut-phase parameters with compressed MRV: if an athlete cannot sustain performance at those reduced volumes, a diet break may be the correct intervention, not a training adjustment.

topics.title: HRV and Autonomic Recovery Signals
topics.body: Heart rate variability (SDNN/rMSSD) measured during sleep as the Autonomic Recovery Condition (ARC) score, z-score normalization against a 30-day rolling baseline, and the fundamental limits of autonomic markers for hypertrophy training where local mechanical tension dominates over central cardiovascular strain.

topics.title: Readiness Bands and Composite Index
topics.body: Four operational readiness bands (High/Peaking, Normal/Baseline, Low, Depleted) defined by the composite Readiness Index formula (RI = 0.6 × ARC + 0.4 × subjective), with per-band volume multipliers and RPE caps that gate daily session intensity without overriding mesocycle volume plans.

topics.title: Multi-Metric Priority Cascade
topics.body: Strictly ordered daily gating hierarchy that prevents noisy HRV signals from corrupting prescriptions: safety red-flags (pain, illness, injury) take absolute precedence, followed by subjective recovery composite, then ARC z-score, then prior-day EWMA acute load residual.

topics.title: Session Autoregulation and Low-Readiness Protocol
topics.body: Deterministic intra-session adjustment rules (RIR miss correction, fatigue drop-off termination) and the 6-step low-readiness day modification algorithm that applies RPE ceilings, trims accessories before compounds, swaps high axial-load exercises, and falls through to technique-only sessions or recommended rest.

topics.title: MEV Floor Protection
topics.body: Volume Deficit Ledger (VDL) that tracks cumulative per-muscle set deficits, suspends set-trimming on compounds when MEV is threatened by day 5 of the microcycle, and triggers a Reactive Micro-Deload if low readiness persists beyond 72 consecutive hours to prevent chronic under-dosing.

topics.title: Deload Policy and Execution
topics.body: Scheduled deloads at fixed mesocycle boundaries (4–6 week cycles), reactive deloads triggered by autonomic suppression, performance regression, or joint discomfort thresholds, severity-graded parameter profiles for sets/intensity/RIR, nutritional-phase modulation, and post-deload landmark resets for volume, load, and ARC baseline.

topics.title: ACWR Workload Monitoring and Spike Guards
topics.body:
Helm computes an EWMA acute:chronic workload ratio (7-day acute, 28-day chronic) and can display it. Literature does not support using that ratio to predict injury or to cancel sessions. Skip-gating from an ACWR spike is behind a flag and is off by default.

Readiness still trims volume on depleted days through the cheapest-first cascade (cap RPE, then isolation, then compounds at the MEV floor). ACWR is a readout, not a veto, unless you turn the experimental skip flag on.

topics.title: RPE and RIR Calibration
topics.body: Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) maps directly to Reps in Reserve (RIR): RPE 6 = 4 RIR, RPE 7 = 3 RIR, RPE 8 = 2 RIR, RPE 9 = 1 RIR, RPE 10 = 0 RIR (failure). Stimulus credit is graded rather than binary: full credit through RIR 2, then a taper, then zero from RIR 6 (warmup). Calibration improves with training experience; novices tend to underestimate RIR (leave more reps than perceived).

topics.title: Movement-Class Progression Engines
topics.body: Three distinct progression engines match the biomechanical and fatigue profiles of different movement classes. Load-First (squat/hinge) prioritizes load before reps. Standard Double Progression (horizontal/vertical press) balances rep expansion and load increments. Rep-First (isolation) and Dynamic Rep-Range (pulls) prioritize rep accumulation before load jumps. Load step sizes vary: +2.5 kg for compounds, +1.25 kg for presses/isolation, reflecting the force-production ceiling of smaller muscle groups.

topics.title: Double Progression Algorithm
topics.body: The core progression algorithm: hold load static while expanding reps to R_max at target RIR across all prescribed sets. Once all sets achieve R_max, increment load by the movement-class step size and reset reps to R_min. Variations include Rep-First (staggered set-by-set rep expansion) and Load-First (load increment prioritized over rep expansion). This ensures every load increase is earned through demonstrated rep-volume expansion, preventing premature intensity escalation and form degradation.

topics.title: Stall Detection and Micro-Reset
topics.body: Stall detection uses a 2-exposure rule for intermediate and advanced lifters. A stall is confirmed when an exercise fails to progress in reps or load across two consecutive sessions at or above target RIR. The prescribed action is a 10% load micro-reset (W_new = W × 0.90) with RIR reset to 3, followed by resumed progression from the new baseline. Volume-based stall solutions (adding sets) increase fatigue without addressing the underlying adaptive stall and are avoided. Novices use a 3-exposure threshold due to higher session-to-session variability.

topics.title: 1RM Estimation and Strength Tracking
topics.body: Estimated 1RM uses the Epley formula (w × (1 + r/30)) computed from submaximal sets within 0-4 RIR. Historical e1RM data decays at λ = 0.005/day after 14 days to model detraining during layoffs. Initial working loads for new exercises are derived from time-decayed e1RM by reversing the Epley equation. This submaximal approach avoids the injury risk and program disruption of direct 1RM testing while providing a reliable longitudinal strength metric for progression decisions.

topics.title: Experience-Tier Progression Architecture
topics.body: Progression parameters differ by training age. Novices (<1 yr, high neural adaptation rate) use fixed weekly load increments with wide rep windows and a lenient 3-exposure stall threshold. Intermediates (1-4 yrs) use standard double progression per movement class with 2-exposure stall. Advanced lifters (>4 yrs, diminishing adaptation rate) require micro-periodized wave loading: alternating high-load/low-rep and low-load/high-rep sessions: with micro-scaled load jumps (+1.0 kg) and a 2-exposure stall threshold. These tiers are set during onboarding but only apply at mesocycle boundaries, never mid-block.

topics.title: Autoregulation, Readiness Gating, and Deload Policy
topics.body: Session intensity and volume auto-adjust via a 5-tier precedence order based on ARC readiness: increase RIR → reduce load → trim isolation sets → drop pattern slots → truncate to maintenance volume. Deloads occur on schedule (every 4-6 weeks) or reactively (e1RM drop >5%, persistent soreness 4/4, or ARC < 0.40 for 3 days). RIR follows a structured ramp across the mesocycle (W1 3 RIR → Peak 0-1 RIR). MEV floor protection prevents readiness gating from depressing volume below MEV for 2+ consecutive weeks.

topics.title: Pain Neuroscience Fundamentals
topics.body: Distinction between nociception (peripheral danger signaling) and pain (CNS protective output). Central sensitization produces allodynia and hyperalgesia in persistent pain states. The Explain Pain framework uses pain neuroscience education to reduce catastrophizing and threat perception.

topics.title: Fear-Avoidance and Psychological Factors
topics.body: The Fear-Avoidance Model explains how catastrophic pain interpretation triggers kinesiophobia and protective avoidance, leading to disuse syndrome and a vicious cycle of worsening pain. Catastrophic coaching language induces nocebo effects. The biopsychosocial model integrates psychological readiness and social context into rehab.

topics.title: Load Management and Tissue Capacity
topics.body: The training-injury prevention paradox: athletes with high chronic workloads have lower injury risk. Danger comes from acute spikes relative to chronic baseline (ACWR). Rehab rebuilds tissue capacity through controlled progressive loading, not rest. Complete rest reduces chronic workload base, creating re-injury risk on return.

topics.title: Tendinopathy Rehabilitation Protocol
topics.body: Tendons respond to mechanical load via mechanotransduction. Complete rest is contraindicated. The progressive loading hierarchy: Phase 1 (Analgesia) heavy isometrics for pain relief; Phase 2 (Strength) Heavy Slow Resistance with 3-4s tempos; Phase 3 (Energy Storage) controlled plyometrics; Phase 4 sport-specific return. Isometric analgesia can be used in-season to manage acute tendon flare-ups.

topics.title: Exercise Regression and Movement Substitution
topics.body: When pain limits an exercise, apply the regression hierarchy in order: (1) reduce Load/volume; (2) slow Speed/tempo; (3) restrict Range of Motion to pain-free angles; (4) reduce Complexity (bilateral to unilateral, barbell to dumbbell); (5) change Movement Vector to shift stress to different synergists. Goal is to maintain the highest possible training effect while keeping pain at 3 to 4 out of 10 or less.

topics.title: Return to Training and Performance Frameworks
topics.body: RTS is a continuum: Return to Participation, Return to Sport, Return to Performance. The StARRT framework balances tissue health, psychological readiness, and contextual factors. Psychological readiness (fear of re-injury) is often the primary barrier. Closed-skill tests (hop distance, dynamometry) must be supplemented with open-skill reactive agility under fatigue before full clearance. Graded exposure systematically reintroduces feared movements.

topics.title: Scope of Practice, Screening, and Safety Boundaries
topics.body: Coaches must not provide medical diagnoses use functional movement constraint labels, never clinical pathology terms. Refer when: pain is 7 out of 10 or above during training, or joint pain persists more than 3 weeks despite pattern substitutions. Movement screening tools (FMS) should individualize exercise prescription, not predict injury or pathologize movement. Limb asymmetry above 15 percent warrants 1.5x volume for the lagging limb matched to the weaker side's capacity. Be vigilant for serious pathology red flags: cauda equina, spinal malignancy, infection, fracture.

topics.title: Regional Joint Stress Mapping and Mandatory Substitutions
topics.body: Specific pain presentations map to prohibited movement patterns and biomechanically safe engine substitutions. Subacromial impingement: avoid overhead pressing above 90 degrees abduction, substitute neutral-grip dumbbell press or landmine press. Patellar tendinopathy: avoid forward-translating knee squats, substitute Spanish squats or box squats with vertical shin vector. Flexion-intolerant lumbar: avoid bent-over barbell rows, substitute chest-supported rows or seated cable rows. Distal biceps tendinopathy: avoid straight-bar curls, substitute hammer curls or cable Bayesian curls.

topics.title: Energy Systems and Metabolic Demands
topics.body: How the ATP-PCr, glycolytic, and oxidative systems work concurrently from exercise onset, why the aerobic crossover occurs around 75 seconds, and why a robust aerobic base is a prerequisite: not an antagonist: for sustaining high training volumes and recovering between intense bouts.

topics.title: The Interference Effect: History and Modern Understanding
topics.body: The 1980 Hickson study that birthed the 'cardio kills gains' dogma, why its extreme 11-session/week protocol exaggerated the effect, and how modern meta-analyses reveal interference is specific to explosive power: not hypertrophy or maximal strength: and is primarily a CNS/neurological phenomenon manageable through session separation.

topics.title: AMPK vs. mTORC1 Molecular Antagonism
topics.body: The intracellular signaling conflict at the heart of the interference effect: endurance training activates AMPK (the energy sensor that halts anabolic processes), strength training activates mTORC1 (the master driver of muscle protein synthesis), and AMPK directly inhibits mTORC1. Temporal separation of 3+ hours: ideally 24: allows AMPK to return to baseline so mTORC1 can respond fully to the lifting stimulus.

topics.title: Training Status Modulation and Sex Differences
topics.body: How interference severity depends on training age and biological sex: untrained individuals experience zero interference due to wide adaptive bandwidth; trained males show moderate lower-body strength blunting and high explosive power interference; trained females show no strength interference at all, likely due to higher Type I fiber proportion, greater fatigue resistance, and faster recovery between sessions.

topics.title: Modality Selection: Running vs. Cycling vs. Rowing
topics.body: Running causes eccentric muscle damage and localized inflammation that directly competes with recovery from lower-body resistance training, measurably blunting strength and hypertrophy. Cycling and rowing are predominantly concentric, low-impact modalities that deliver central (stroke volume, cardiac output) and peripheral (mitochondrial biogenesis) adaptations without the mechanical trauma. For the strength athlete, low-impact modalities are unequivocally superior for preserving lower-body gains.

topics.title: Minimum Effective Dose for Health and Longevity
topics.body: 90 minutes/week of moderate activity delivers a 14% all-cause mortality reduction and 3 years of added life expectancy. 150 minutes/week pushes cardiovascular mortality reduction past 20–30%. For the strength-focused athlete, 2–3 weekly 30-minute LISS sessions (cycling, incline walking) easily hit this dose without generating the CNS fatigue, glycogen depletion, or mechanical damage that triggers interference: rendering it entirely safe for preserving maximal strength and hypertrophy.

topics.title: Polarized Training Intensity Distribution
topics.body: The 80/20 model used by elite endurance athletes: ~80% of sessions at strictly low intensity (Zone 1, below LT1, <2 mmol/L lactate) and ~15–20% at very high intensity (Zone 3, above LT2, >4 mmol/L). Zone 2 'grey zone' training (between thresholds, 2–4 mmol/L) is deliberately avoided: it's intense enough to deplete glycogen and elevate cortisol but not intense enough to drive maximal stroke volume or VO₂max adaptations. For the concurrent athlete, polarized distribution preserves adaptive reserve for strength training while delivering superior endurance outcomes.

topics.title: Respiratory Muscle Metaboreflex and Fatigue Management
topics.body: During heavy sustained exercise, a fatigued diaphragm triggers the respiratory muscle metaboreflex: a protective reflex that constricts blood vessels in the working limbs to redirect cardiac output to the struggling respiratory muscles. The athlete experiences sudden, severe leg fatigue that originates from respiratory insufficiency, not muscular failure. Inspiratory Muscle Training (IMT, breathing against resistance) strengthens the diaphragm, delaying metaboreflex activation and preserving limb blood flow. Self-Myofascial Release (foam rolling) improves tissue perfusion and lactate clearance between sessions.

topics.title: Mind-Muscle Connection & Attentional Focus
topics.body: How your cognitive focus: internal (on the muscle) vs external (on the outcome): alters neuromuscular recruitment, force output, and long-term adaptation. The right focus depends entirely on load and goal.

topics.title: Unilateral Training & Stability Myths
topics.body: Why unilateral work is essential for structural balance but can't replace bilateral lifts for max strength: and why unstable surface training (BOSU balls, balance boards) is actively counterproductive for strength and hypertrophy.

topics.body: Why resistance training is safer than most sports, how to distinguish ugly-but-safe reps from dangerous form breakdown, and when to accept form degradation on near-failure sets.
